{{short description|Method of multiple regression analysis used in behavioural genetics}}
{{Regression bar}}
In [[behavioural genetics]], '''DeFries–Fulker (DF) regression''', also sometimes called '''DeFries–Fulker extremes analysis''', is a type of [[multiple regression analysis]] designed for estimating the magnitude of genetic and environmental effects in [[twin studies]].<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |title=DeFries–Fulker Analysis |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons, Ltd]] |location=Chichester, UK |last1=Rende |first1=Richard |date=2005-10-15 |language=en |doi=10.1002/0470013192.bsa165 |isbn=978-0470860809 |last2=Slomkowski |first2=Cheryl |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Statistics in Behavioral Science}}</ref> It is named after [[John C. DeFries]] and [[David Fulker]], who first proposed it in 1985.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=DeFries |first1=J. C. |author-link=John C. DeFries |last2=Fulker |first2=D. W. |author-link2=David Fulker |date=September 1985 |title=Multiple regression analysis of twin data |journal=[[Behavior Genetics (journal)|Behavior Genetics]] |language=en |volume=15 |issue=5 |pages=467–473 |doi=10.1007/bf01066239 |issn=0001-8244 |pmid=4074272|s2cid=1172312 }}</ref> It was originally developed to assess [[heritability]] of [[reading disability]] in twin studies, but it has since been used to assess the heritability of other cognitive traits, and has also been applied to non-twin methodologies.<ref name=pps/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rodgers |first1=Joseph Lee |author-link=Joseph Lee Rodgers |last2=McGue |first2=Matt |author-link2=Matt McGue |date=May 1994 |title=A simple algebraic demonstration of the validity of DeFries–Fulker analysis in unselected samples with multiple kinship levels |journal=Behavior Genetics |language=en |volume=24 |issue=3 |pages=259–262 |doi=10.1007/bf01067192 |pmid=7945155 |s2cid=37412119 |issn=0001-8244}}</ref>

==Approach==
DeFries–Fulker regression analysis is based on the differences in the magnitude of [[regression to the mean]] in a genetic trait between [[monozygotic twins|monozygotic]] (MZ) and [[dizygotic twins|dizygotic]] (DZ) twins. In DF regression, the first step is to select [[proband]]s in a twin study with extreme scores on the trait being studied, and to regression to the mean among their co-twins depending on whether the probands are part of a MZ or DZ twin pair. DF regression is thus based on the assumption that, to the extent that genetic factors play a role in causing the extreme variation in the studied trait, the magnitude of regression to the mean should be greater in DZ co-twins of probands than in their MZ counterparts.<ref name=colorado>{{Cite web |url=http://psych.colorado.edu/~willcutt/CLDRC/DFanalysis.htm |title=DeFries-Fulker multiple regression analysis |website=Erik Willcutt website|publisher=[[University of Colorado Boulder]] |access-date=2018-06-20}}</ref> This should result in MZ co-twins being more similar to their probands on the trait under study than DZ twins are to theirs.<ref name=pps/>

===Modifications===
Since the DF regression approach was first proposed in 1985, other researchers have proposed modified versions of the DF model that take additional factors into account, including observed covariates<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lazzeroni |first1=Laura C. |last2=Ray |first2=Amrita |date=2012-12-20 |title=A Generalized Defries–Fulker Regression Framework for the Analysis of Twin Data |journal=Behavior Genetics |language=en |volume=43 |issue=1 |pages=85–96 |doi=10.1007/s10519-012-9573-7 |issn=0001-8244 |pmc=3573860 |pmid=23264207}}</ref> and opposite-sex DZ twins.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Purcell |first1=S. |authorlink=Shaun Purcell|last2=Sham |first2=P.C.|authorlink2=Pak Sham|date=2003 |title=A Model-Fitting Implementation of the DeFries–Fulker Model for Selected Twin Data |journal=Behavior Genetics |language=en |volume=33 |issue=3 |pages=271–278 |doi=10.1023/a:1023494408079 |pmid=12837017 |s2cid=42718780 |issn=0001-8244}}</ref>

==Regression analysis==
The probands are chosen with scores that fall below a "cutoff" for what is considered "extreme", and regression is then used to predict the co-twin scores based on those of the probands and a term reflecting whether the twin pair is MZ (1.0) or DZ (0.5).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bishop |first=D. V. M. |author-link=Dorothy V. M. Bishop |date=July 2005 |title=DeFries–Fulker analysis of twin data with skewed distributions: cautions and recommendations from a study of children's use of verb inflections  |journal=Behavior Genetics |volume=35 |issue=4 |pages=479–490 |doi=10.1007/s10519-004-1834-7 |issn=0001-8244 |pmid=15971028|s2cid=37088113 }}</ref> The formula used for DF regression is:

:{{math|''C'' {{=}} ''B''<sub>1</sub>''P'' + ''B''<sub>2</sub>''R'' + ''K''}}

where ''C'' = expected co-twin score, ''P'' = proband score, ''R'' = coefficient of relationship (0.5 for DZ twins, 1.0 for MZ twins), and ''K'' = regression constant. ''B''<sub>1</sub> represents a measure of co-twin relatedness separate from that of zygosity, while ''B''<sub>2</sub> can be converted into an estimate of the [[heritability]] of extreme scores on the trait.<ref name=colorado/> By comparing MZ and DZ co-twins in this manner, an estimate of "group heritability" is generated.<ref name=pps>{{Cite journal |last1=Plomin |first1=Robert|authorlink=Robert Plomin |last2=DeFries |first2=John C. |last3=Knopik |first3=Valerie S. |last4=Neiderhiser |first4=Jenae M. |authorlink4=Jenae Neiderhiser|date=January 2016 |title=Top 10 Replicated Findings From Behavioral Genetics |journal=[[Perspectives on Psychological Science]] |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=3–23 |doi=10.1177/1745691615617439 |issn=1745-6916 |pmc=4739500 |pmid=26817721}}</ref>
